processing: Mature shoots are cut and sun-dried, then chopped, sieved, blended, steamed and piled. The tea is weighed, stir-fried and rammed hot into a bamboo-strip bale, which is stacked to heat for 4 to 6 days and then aired for 20 to 30 days.
harvest_season: Summer, when one- to two-year-old mature shoots are cut with a blade. Tender picking plays no part in this tea.
appearance_dry: A squared bamboo-strip bale of yellow-brown, very stalky tea, with stems making up around 60% of the content.
appearance_wet: Coarse yellow-brown leaf mixed with plenty of cut stem.
taste_profile: Mellow and plain, with a slightly smoky, scorched aroma. The colour runs deeper than the flavour.

brewing.notes: As with other coarse border teas, simmering suits it better than quick steeps. Stems give up their flavour slowly, so a short steep tastes thin.

vintage_note: This is a border-trade tea sold by the bale or broken down from bales, usually without the season language used for fine tea. Like other Sichuan dark teas it keeps well, and any age claim is worth checking against the producer and the packing. It is not a tea to buy as a fresh harvest.
description:
Fangbao Cha is the main product of Sichuan's West Road border tea, from the old Guan county around Dujiangyan. The name simply means square bale, because the tea is rammed into a rectangular bamboo-strip package.

It is about as coarse as tea gets. The raw material is cut branch tips, sun-dried and later steamed and piled before being fried and packed hot. The hot bales are then stacked so that they keep heating, and that step, followed by weeks of airing, sets the yellow-brown colour and the faint scorched note.

Expect a mellow cup with little sweetness or perfume, more stalk and smoke than leaf. Treat it as a tea to simmer rather than a gongfu tea, and do not judge it by the standards of a tender leaf.

The old specification is a large one: a bale of about 35 kg is commonly given, though 37 kg also appears, and neither is a size most drinkers would ever buy whole. A smaller retail portion should still look stalky and yellow-brown; that is the style, not a fault.
history:
Fangbao belongs to the West Road border teas made around Guan county and Beichuan for sale to frontier regions. Guan county made the rectangular bale, while Beichuan made a round one; the round bale later ended and production moved to the fangbao specification.

The tea travelled by horse, two bales to an animal, which gave it the other name Ma Cha, horse tea. No clear founding date is on record.
